Reference: Aspelund and Russo (2026)

Model Setting

The paper studies additionality as a problem of asymmetric information in markets for environmental services. A conservation contract is socially valuable only to the extent that it changes behavior, but landowners who would have conserved anyway tend to have low costs of accepting a contract and therefore win procurement mechanisms that screen on cost alone. The setting is the USDA's Conservation Reserve Program (CRP), one of the largest payments for ecosystem services (PES) schemes in the world, which pays landowners 1.6 to 1.8 billion dollars per year to retire cropland and undertake conservation actions under (typically ten-year) contracts. Contracts are allocated in a discriminatory, asymmetric scoring auction. The authors link confidential administrative data on all bids in the seven general-enrollment auctions of 2009-2021 to field-level land use from the 30-m Cropland Data Layer (2009-2020) and administrative Form 578 data (2013-2019), with aerial imagery to verify compliance. The paper has three parts: a stylized framework in the spirit of Einav, Finkelstein and Cullen (2010) showing that the cost distribution and an additionality function are sufficient statistics for welfare; reduced-form evidence that only about one quarter of marginal winners are additional and that additionality is positively correlated with bids (adverse selection); and a structural model of multidimensional bidding and additionality used to evaluate welfare under alternative auctions and scoring rules.

Stylized Framework

A continuum of landowners iii each decides whether to contract, xi∈{0,1}x_i\in\{0,1\}xi​∈{0,1}, in exchange for a transfer ppp. The contract requires an environmental action ai=1a_i=1ai​=1 (land retirement) rather than ai=0a_i=0ai​=0 (cropping), and the action generates social benefits B>0B>0B>0. Let ai1a_{i1}ai1​ and ai0a_{i0}ai0​ be the actions with and without the contract. With perfect compliance, ai1=1a_{i1}=1ai1​=1, so the benefit of contracting with iii is only the increment B⋅(1−ai0)B\cdot(1-a_{i0})B⋅(1−ai0​); ai0a_{i0}ai0​ is never observed for contracted landowners and is therefore noncontractible. Each landowner has type θi=(ci,ai0)\theta_i=(c_i,a_{i0})θi​=(ci​,ai0​) drawn from F(θ)F(\theta)F(θ), where cic_ici​ is the minimum transfer she needs to accept the contract (the forgone option value of cropping over the contract period plus hassle costs). Landowners who expect low cropping payoffs both have low cic_ici​ and are likely to conserve anyway, so cic_ici​ and ai0a_{i0}ai0​ are correlated. The key object is the conditional expectation of additionality given cost:

τ(c)=E[1−ai0∣c=ci](9.4.2.1)\tau(c)=\mathbb{E}\left[1-a_{i0}\mid c=c_i\right] \tag{9.4.2.1}τ(c)=E[1−ai0​∣c=ci​](9.4.2.1)

The social surplus of contracting with iii and her private decision at price ppp are:

SSi=B⋅(1−ai0)−ci(9.4.2.2)SS_i=B\cdot(1-a_{i0})-c_i \tag{9.4.2.2}SSi​=B⋅(1−ai0​)−ci​(9.4.2.2)

The landowner transacts on ppp and cic_ici​ only, while social surplus also depends on 1−ai01-a_{i0}1−ai0​. The socially optimal uniform price solves:

Hence fCf_CfC​ and τ(c)\tau(c)τ(c) are sufficient statistics for welfare (and, following Lopomo, Persico and Villa (2023), for any incentive-compatible mechanism). The efficient allocation contracts with iii whenever:

B⋅τ(ci)−ci≥0(9.4.2.5)B\cdot\tau(c_i)-c_i\geq 0 \tag{9.4.2.5}B⋅τ(ci​)−ci​≥0(9.4.2.5)

Graphically, with qqq the population share ranked by cost, the marginal cost curve is FC−1(q)F_C^{-1}(q)FC−1​(q) and the contract value curve is B⋅τ(FC−1(q))B\cdot\tau(F_C^{-1}(q))B⋅τ(FC−1​(q)), which lies weakly below BBB. An upward-sloping contract value curve (τ′(c)>0\tau'(c)>0τ′(c)>0) represents adverse selection. If B⋅τ(c)−cB\cdot\tau(c)-cB⋅τ(c)−c is decreasing in ccc, the efficient allocation is implemented by the price p∗p^*p∗ that solves p∗=B⋅τ(p∗)p^*=B\cdot\tau(p^*)p∗=B⋅τ(p∗), and pricing at BBB (ignoring counterfactual land use) creates welfare losses. If instead B⋅τ(c)−cB\cdot\tau(c)-cB⋅τ(c)−c crosses zero from below, the lowest-cost landowners are the least valuable, the efficient allocation would require an allocation rule that is not monotonically decreasing in cost, and no mechanism can implement it (Myerson 1981); it may even be optimal to have no market.

Auction Rules

Eligible landowners (who meet erosion standards, lie in a conservation priority area, and cropped at least four years in a five- to ten-year window before the auction, or are reenrolling) bid for heterogeneous contracts that "top up" the base action of land retirement with actions such as specific grass mixes, trees, or pollinator and rare habitats. A known scoring rule (in USDA practice, the Environmental Benefits Index) awards points for the environmental sensitivity of the land (erodibility, habitat importance, water and air quality, carbon), for the chosen contract, and for a low bid rental rate in dollars per acre per year, subject to a bid cap based on county rental rates and soil productivity. Congress fixes aggregate acreage in the Farm Bill, which determines the winning-score threshold; all bids scoring above it win. Because acreage and competitors are uncertain, bidders face uncertainty about the threshold. Crucially, the scoring rule is built under the assumption that land would be cropped absent the program, i.e. full additionality. Early exit or noncompliance is penalized by refunding all payments plus 25 percent. The average auction has 36,772 bidders; the average bidder offers 84.1 acres (33 percent of her land) at 83 dollars per acre-year, 70 percent are recontracting, and 81 percent win.

Reduced-Form Evidence on Additionality

The paper uses a regression discontinuity (RD) design at the winning-score threshold. For bidder iii in auction ggg and year ttt:

yigt=βr(i,t)⋅1{Sig≥S‾g}+fr(i,t)(Sig−S‾g)+νigt(9.4.2.6)y_{igt}=\beta_{r(i,t)}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{S_{ig}\geq\underline{S}_g\}+f_{r(i,t)}\left(S_{ig}-\underline{S}_g\right)+\nu_{igt} \tag{9.4.2.6}yigt​=βr(i,t)​⋅1{Sig​≥S​g​}+fr(i,t)​(Sig​−S​g​)+νigt​(9.4.2.6)

where SigS_{ig}Sig​ is the score, S‾g\underline{S}_gS​g​ the threshold, r(i,t)=t−tg(i)r(i,t)=t-t_{g(i)}r(i,t)=t−tg(i)​ the year relative to the auction, and fr(i,t)(⋅)f_{r(i,t)}(\cdot)fr(i,t)​(⋅) relative-year-specific local-linear functions in the MSE-optimal bandwidth of Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014). The pooled version is:

yigt=β⋅1{Sig≥S‾g}+f(Sig−S‾g)+νigt(9.4.2.7)y_{igt}=\beta\cdot\mathbf{1}\{S_{ig}\geq\underline{S}_g\}+f\left(S_{ig}-\underline{S}_g\right)+\nu_{igt} \tag{9.4.2.7}yigt​=β⋅1{Sig​≥S​g​}+f(Sig​−S​g​)+νigt​(9.4.2.7)

estimated for r(i,t)>0r(i,t)>0r(i,t)>0 on five auctions (2010-2016) with post-auction land use, at the landowner level, clustering by bidder. There is no bunching at the threshold and no pre-auction difference in cropping (placebo coefficients 0.002 and 0.004). The first stage for receiving a contract is close to one, and winners contract 0.345 of their land. Winners crop 7.5 (remote sensing) or 9.7 (administrative) percentage points less of their land post-auction, and the freed land goes to natural vegetation and grassland (+0.091). Effects grow in the first two years and are then flat over the ten-year contract. Marginal additionality is the ratio of the land use effect to the share contracted (the benchmark in which all marginal winners are additional, τ=1\tau=1τ=1):

τ^RD=−β^ croppedβ^ contracted(9.4.2.8)\hat{\tau}_{RD}=\frac{-\hat{\beta}^{\,\text{cropped}}}{\hat{\beta}^{\,\text{contracted}}} \tag{9.4.2.8}τ^RD​=β^​contracted−β^​cropped​(9.4.2.8)

This gives 22-23 percent (remote sensing) and 28-29 percent (administrative), and 26 percent using natural vegetation: three quarters of marginal winners are not additional. Additionality strictly between 0 and 1 rejects a single-index model in which costs and additionality coincide, and cross-auction thresholds give marginal additionality of 12 to 42 percent, increasing in the quantile of the marginal bidder, consistent with an upward-sloping B⋅τB\cdot\tauB⋅τ curve. Aerial photographs show no noncompliance and there are no spillovers to nonbid fields (coefficient −0.007-0.007−0.007), so for every losing bidder the land use on bid fields measures 1−ai01-a_{i0}1−ai0​.

Testing for Asymmetric Information

In the 2016 auction, where bid fields are delineated and 82 percent of bidders lose, the authors run a positive-correlation test in the spirit of Chiappori and Salanie (2000) and Hendricks and Porter (1988):

1−ai0=β⋅bi+π⋅zi+h(zis)+νi(9.4.2.9)1-a_{i0}=\beta\cdot\mathbf{b}_i+\pi\cdot\mathbf{z}_i+h(\mathbf{z}_i^s)+\nu_i \tag{9.4.2.9}1−ai0​=β⋅bi​+π⋅zi​+h(zis​)+νi​(9.4.2.9)

where 1−ai01-a_{i0}1−ai0​ is the share of rejected bidder iii's bid fields that are cropped, bi\mathbf{b}_ibi​ are bid characteristics, h(zis)h(\mathbf{z}_i^s)h(zis​) controls for the scoring-rule characteristics, and zi\mathbf{z}_izi​ are other characteristics. Three facts emerge: (1) additionality is heterogeneous and rises with the bid rental rate, also conditional on prior land use interacted with soil productivity, i.e. adverse selection on private costs; (2) contract choice reveals additionality, with markedly lower additionality on tree-related contracts relative to introduced grasses; (3) USDA estimates of soil productivity, which are not in the scoring rule, predict additionality.

Model: Types and Additionality

There are NNN landowners and JJJ contracts. Landowner iii has costs (ci,κi)(c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)(ci​,κi​) with κi={κij}\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i=\{\kappa_{ij}\}κi​={κij​}: the cost of contract jjj is ci+κijc_i+\kappa_{ij}ci​+κij​, where cic_ici​ is the base cost common to all contracts and κij\kappa_{ij}κij​ the top-up cost of contract jjj. The type is θi=((ci,κi),ai0)\theta_i=((c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i),a_{i0})θi​=((ci​,κi​),ai0​) with distribution F(θ)F(\theta)F(θ) and cost marginal Fc,κF_{c,\kappa}Fc,κ​; costs are independent across landowners conditional on observables zi\mathbf{z}_izi​. Additionality generalizes to:

τ(zi,ci,κi)=E[1−ai0∣zi,ci,κi](9.4.2.10)\tau(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)=\mathbb{E}\left[1-a_{i0}\mid\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i\right] \tag{9.4.2.10}τ(zi​,ci​,κi​)=E[1−ai0​∣zi​,ci​,κi​](9.4.2.10)

The paper models this conditional expectation directly rather than the choice of ai0a_{i0}ai0​: together with Fc,κF_{c,\kappa}Fc,κ​ it suffices for welfare in any counterfactual that holds the contract menu fixed.

Model: Bidding

A bid is bi=(ri,xi)\mathbf{b}_i=(r_i,\mathbf{x}_i)bi​=(ri​,xi​): a rental rate rir_iri​ in dollars per acre-year and a contract vector with xij=1x_{ij}=1xij​=1 for the chosen contract and ∑jxij=1\sum_j x_{ij}=1∑j​xij​=1. The bid is converted into a score s(bi,zis)s(\mathbf{b}_i,\mathbf{z}_i^s)s(bi​,zis​), decreasing in rrr, and all bids above the threshold S‾\underline{S}S​ win. Landowners do not observe their competitors and share common beliefs about the threshold:

G(S)=Pr⁡{S≥S‾}(9.4.2.11)G(S)=\Pr\left\{S\geq\underline{S}\right\} \tag{9.4.2.11}G(S)=Pr{S≥S​}(9.4.2.11)

which integrate over rivals' strategies, the number of bidders, and the acreage limit. Each landowner solves:

bi∗=arg⁡max⁡(r,x){(r−ci−x⋅κi)×G(s((r,x),zis))}(9.4.2.12)\mathbf{b}_i^*=\arg\max_{(r,\mathbf{x})}\left\{\left(r-c_i-\mathbf{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i\right)\times G\left(s\left((r,\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{z}_i^s\right)\right)\right\} \tag{9.4.2.12}bi∗​=arg(r,x)max​{(r−ci​−x⋅κi​)×G(s((r,x),zis​))}(9.4.2.12)

Since winning depends only on the score, the best response splits into an inner problem and an outer problem (Che 1993; Asker and Cantillon 2008). Let r(S,x,zis)r(S,\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}_i^s)r(S,x,zis​) be the payment that reaches score SSS with contract x\mathbf{x}x, defined by s((r(S,x,zis),x),zis)=Ss((r(S,\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}_i^s),\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{z}_i^s)=Ss((r(S,x,zis​),x),zis​)=S; this is the menu of payments the scoring rule offers per contract. The inner problem picks the best contract for each target score:

These discrete best-response conditions play the role of the first-order condition in Guerre, Perrigne and Vuong (2000) and act as a bid inversion into bounds on costs. and a downward deviation gives the opposite bound, so higher-cost landowners choose lower scores. The inner problem bounds κi\boldsymbol{\kappa}_iκi​ through relative payments across contracts, and the outer problem bounds ci+xi∗(Si∗)⋅κic_i+\mathbf{x}_i^*(S_i^*)\cdot\boldsymbol{\kappa}_ici​+xi∗​(Si∗​)⋅κi​. The source of inefficiency is the same as in the stylized model: bids and allocations depend on s(bi,zis)s(\mathbf{b}_i,\mathbf{z}_i^s)s(bi​,zis​) and (ci,κi)(c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)(ci​,κi​), but the efficient allocation also depends on τ(zi,ci,κi)\tau(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)τ(zi​,ci​,κi​).

Identification

Given beliefs and the scoring rule, the inequalities link observed bids to costs (Agarwal, Li and Somaini 2023), but individual costs are not point-identified: the cost vector has dimension JJJ while the bid reveals one contract and one score. Nonparametric identification of Fc,κ∣zF_{c,\kappa\mid z}Fc,κ∣z​ would require full-support variation in the payment vector r(S,x,zis)r(S,\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}_i^s)r(S,x,zis​) across contracts and scores. For τ(⋅)\tau(\cdot)τ(⋅), the ideal experiment is a "cancelled auction": if all bidders were unexpectedly rejected, E[1−ai0∣zi,bi∗]\mathbb{E}[1-a_{i0}\mid\mathbf{z}_i,\mathbf{b}_i^*]E[1−ai0​∣zi​,bi∗​] would be observed for everyone and the best-response inequalities would map bids into costs. In practice, ai0a_{i0}ai0​ is missing for winners (18 percent even in 2016). The paper therefore combines scoring-rule variation with parametric extrapolation. The variation is: (i) a mid-mechanism change in 2021, when carbon-based payments were announced and bids re-collected, raising the payment needed for a given score by 3, 5 or 10 percent depending on the contract; (ii) after 2011, 30 Wildlife Priority Zone (WPZ) points are awarded only for a subset of contracts; and (iii) Air Quality Zone (AQZ) status shifts the level of the score. These shifts (about 8 dollars for affected contracts under the WPZ change) are modest relative to threshold differences across auctions (over 20 dollars between the average and the 2016 threshold for the base contract). Costs are parameterized as:

ci∼N(c(zi),σc2(zi))κij=pj(zi)+uj(zi)+ϵij,ϵij∼i.i.d.N(0,σκ2(zi))(9.4.2.16)\begin{aligned} c_i&\sim N\left(c(\mathbf{z}_i),\sigma_c^2(\mathbf{z}_i)\right)\\ \kappa_{ij}&=p_j(\mathbf{z}_i)+u_j(\mathbf{z}_i)+\epsilon_{ij},\qquad\epsilon_{ij}\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim}N\left(0,\sigma_\kappa^2(\mathbf{z}_i)\right) \end{aligned} \tag{9.4.2.16}ci​κij​​∼N(c(zi​),σc2​(zi​))=pj​(zi​)+uj​(zi​)+ϵij​,ϵij​∼i.i.d.N(0,σκ2​(zi​))​(9.4.2.16)

where pjp_jpj​ are mean costs of primary covers relative to introduced grasses (normalized to zero) and uju_juj​ are upgrade covers relative to no upgrade (normalized to zero); there are 36 possible contracts. Additionality is linear:

τ(zi,ci,κi)=π⋅zi+β⋅ci+α⋅κi(9.4.2.17)\tau(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)=\pi\cdot\mathbf{z}_i+\beta\cdot c_i+\alpha\cdot\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i \tag{9.4.2.17}τ(zi​,ci​,κi​)=π⋅zi​+β⋅ci​+α⋅κi​(9.4.2.17)

with αj=αj′\alpha_j=\alpha_{j'}αj​=αj′​ whenever pj=pj′p_j=p_{j'}pj​=pj′​ and uj=uj′u_j=u_{j'}uj​=uj′​. The coefficient β\betaβ (and α\alphaα) captures selection on unobserved costs.

Estimation

Step 1 (beliefs). Following Hortacsu (2000) and Hortacsu and McAdams (2010), beta distributions are fit to the number of bidders and acreage limits using auctions from 2000 to 2021; simulated auctions resample observed scores and acreages, and G(S)G(S)G(S) is the share of simulated auctions in which SSS wins.

Step 2 (costs). Fc,κ∣zF_{c,\kappa\mid z}Fc,κ∣z​ is estimated by maximum simulated likelihood: the likelihood of an observed bid is the probability, over simulated draws of (ci,κi)(c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)(ci​,κi​), that the inner and outer inequalities hold, checking all feasible deviations. The observed bid is coarsened to score deciles and seven contract categories (the bidder's problem is solved without coarsening), with importance sampling (Ackerberg 2009). There are 32 observable cells (quartiles of soil productivity by prior CRP status by prior land use), and all auctions are used, including the interim and final 2021 mechanisms.

Step 3 (additionality). (π,β,α)(\pi,\beta,\alpha)(π,β,α) are estimated by the method of simulated moments: draw (cik,κik)(c_i^k,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i^k)(cik​,κik​), solve for the optimal bid bi∗k\mathbf{b}_i^{*k}bi∗k​, and match (i) additionality at the winning-score threshold, (ii) additionality among all rejected bidders and by observables, (iii) the covariance between additionality and chosen scores, and (iv) additionality by chosen contract. The outcome is the share of bid fields cropped in 2017-2020 among rejected bidders in the 2016 auction, assuming τ(⋅)\tau(\cdot)τ(⋅) is stable across auctions. Robustness checks use alternative functional forms and a nonparametric GPV-style inversion holding contract choice fixed.

Key Estimates

  • Costs: the mean base cost is 67.21 dollars per acre-year (92.86 for above-median soil productivity), with many landowners below 50 dollars and a long right tail. Mean top-up costs are −0.03-0.03−0.03 for native grasses, 23.76 for trees, 15.06 for habitat, 15.44 for rare habitat, 18.79 for wildlife food plots and 17.97 for pollinator habitat. Rejected bidders with higher simulated cic_ici​ crop more, an out-of-sample validation of revealed-preference costs.

  • Additionality: with α=0\alpha=0α=0, β\betaβ is 0.0018 (scoring-rule controls) and 0.0017 (adding the 32 cells), so each extra dollar of base cost raises additionality by about 0.2 percentage points. Allowing only tree costs, β=0.0007\beta=0.0007β=0.0007 and the tree coefficient is 0.0025. In the most flexible specification, β=−0.0008\beta=-0.0008β=−0.0008 and the cost-additionality correlation loads on κi\boldsymbol{\kappa}_iκi​ (0.0020 to 0.0034 across covers, largest for trees at 0.0047).

  • Fit: the model-implied additionality at the RD margin is 23 percent, matching the reduced form.

Social Benefits and Welfare

Contract benefits Bj(zis)B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)Bj​(zis​) use average valuations from the CRP literature (habitat, erosion, water and air quality, greenhouse gases), with relative valuations across zis\mathbf{z}_i^szis​ and jjj taken from the scoring rule, which the USDA states assumes τ=1\tau=1τ=1; results can alternatively be read as the USDA's revealed preferences. The expected social surplus of awarding contract jjj to iii is:

Bj(zis)⋅τ(zi,ci,κi)−ci−κij(9.4.2.18)B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)\cdot\tau(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)-c_i-\kappa_{ij} \tag{9.4.2.18}Bj​(zis​)⋅τ(zi​,ci​,κi​)−ci​−κij​(9.4.2.18)

which uses τ(⋅)\tau(\cdot)τ(⋅) rather than 1−ai01-a_{i0}1−ai0​ without loss, since all mechanisms screen only on (zi,ci,κi)(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)(zi​,ci​,κi​). Welfare of an allocation is:

W=∑i∑j(Bj(zis)⋅τ(zi,ci,κi)−ci−κij)⋅xij(9.4.2.19)W=\sum_i\sum_j\left(B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)\cdot\tau(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)-c_i-\kappa_{ij}\right)\cdot x_{ij} \tag{9.4.2.19}W=i∑​j∑​(Bj​(zis​)⋅τ(zi​,ci​,κi​)−ci​−κij​)⋅xij​(9.4.2.19)

In the empirical graphical analysis for the base contract, the contract value curve lies below BBB and slopes up but crosses marginal cost from above, as in the implementable case. The socially optimal uniform price yields gains of 14.37 dollars per acre-year, while pricing at BBB causes losses of 12.68 dollars per acre-year, nearly offsetting them. For tree contracts the contract value curve crosses from below, so efficient gains cannot be implemented without losses on the cheapest (least additional) landowners. Splitting by soil productivity yields different optimal prices.

Counterfactuals: Alternative Auctions

The status quo auction yields 120 million dollars of welfare gains per auction, only 12 percent of the efficient benchmark (984 million), which uses all zi\mathbf{z}_izi​ and (ci,κi)(c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)(ci​,κi​) subject to at most one contract per landowner and no more contracts than the status quo; it awards contracts to 50 percent of bidders (versus 81) with average additionality 0.447 (versus 0.201), but need not be implementable. Counterfactual rules are linear:

sj(zi)=ωz⋅zi+ωj(9.4.2.20)s_j(\mathbf{z}_i)=\omega_z\cdot\mathbf{z}_i+\omega_j \tag{9.4.2.20}sj​(zi​)=ωz​⋅zi​+ωj​(9.4.2.20)

using only immutable observables to avoid gaming. They are implemented as Vickrey auctions with scoring (VCG), which maximize scoring-rule-implied welfare:

∑i∑j(sj(zi)−ci−κij)⋅xij(9.4.2.21)\sum_i\sum_j\left(s_j(\mathbf{z}_i)-c_i-\kappa_{ij}\right)\cdot x_{ij} \tag{9.4.2.21}i∑​j∑​(sj​(zi​)−ci​−κij​)⋅xij​(9.4.2.21)

Bidders report (ci,κi)(c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)(ci​,κi​) truthfully, are ranked by max⁡jsj(zi)−ci−κij\max_j s_j(\mathbf{z}_i)-c_i-\kappa_{ij}maxj​sj​(zi​)−ci​−κij​, and the top bidders up to the quantity limit receive contract ji∗=arg⁡max⁡j{sj(zi)−ci−κij}j_i^*=\arg\max_j\{s_j(\mathbf{z}_i)-c_i-\kappa_{ij}\}ji∗​=argmaxj​{sj​(zi​)−ci​−κij​}. Welfare is always evaluated with the true objective WWW. Results (million dollars per auction): the status quo rule in VCG gives 140 (14 percent of efficient); reweighting contract incentives ωj\omega_jωj​ gives 296 (+156); reweighting existing characteristics ωz\omega_zωz​ gives 333; adding an additionality factor τ^(zi)\hat{\tau}(\mathbf{z}_i)τ^(zi​), a projection of τ(⋅)\tau(\cdot)τ(⋅) on deciles of soil productivity and wind and water erosion, gives 349 (+53 from the asymmetry terms); and reducing quantity by rejecting bidders with max⁡jsj(zi)−ci−κij<0\max_j s_j(\mathbf{z}_i)-c_i-\kappa_{ij}<0maxj​sj​(zi​)−ci​−κij​<0 gives 440 (+91), with 62 percent awarded and USDA spending falling from 1,615 to 877 million. The last rule closes 37 percent of the gap between the status quo and the efficient allocation. A uniform multiplier rule:

sj(zis)=θ⋅Bj(zis)(9.4.2.22)s_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)=\theta\cdot B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s) \tag{9.4.2.22}sj​(zis​)=θ⋅Bj​(zis​)(9.4.2.22)

gives 325, so a single discount for imperfect additionality captures most of the gains; heterogeneous adjustment adds 24 million. Two mechanisms are at work: the status quo rule overweights asymmetries in Bj(zis)B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)Bj​(zis​) that are not realized when land would be conserved anyway, and systematic heterogeneity in additionality can be targeted.

Extensions

  • Status quo format: the preferred scoring rule in the existing discriminatory auction, with beliefs G(S)G(S)G(S) and best responses iterated to a fixed point, gives 236 million without raising USDA spending (1,373 million). Switching to VCG alone adds only 20 million; changing the scoring rule adds over five times as much.

  • Limited-information rule: a rule built only from pre-2016 auctions, using cross-tract cropping heterogeneity and cross-auction RD coefficients in administrative data, gives 217 million in the 2016 holdout auction versus 91 million under the status quo in that year.

  • Spending: across auctions government spending exceeds the environmental value procured because of adverse selection, since the marginal landowner is more additional than inframarginal ones.

  • Welfare weights: the status quo is preferred to the best counterfactual only if a dollar to landowners is worth more than three times a dollar spent on conservation.

  • Alternative benefits: if additionality affects only the base action, contract value becomes B0(zis)⋅τ(zi,ci,κi)+Bj(zis)B_0(\mathbf{z}_i^s)\cdot\tau(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)+B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)B0​(zis​)⋅τ(zi​,ci​,κi​)+Bj​(zis​), with BjB_jBj​ now the incremental top-up value.

This equation defines the additionality function, the central object of the paper. The indicator ai0∈{0,1}a_{i0}\in\{0,1\}ai0​∈{0,1} is the action landowner iii would take without a contract (ai0=1a_{i0}=1ai0​=1 means she would retire the land anyway, ai0=0a_{i0}=0ai0​=0 means she would crop it). Hence 1−ai01-a_{i0}1−ai0​ equals one exactly when the contract changes behavior, and τ(c)\tau(c)τ(c) is the share of landowners with cost ccc whose land would otherwise be cropped. It is a unitless number in [0,1][0,1][0,1].

The conditioning on cost is what matters. A mechanism can only screen landowners on what they reveal through their choices, and choices depend on cic_ici​ alone, so ai0a_{i0}ai0​ enters welfare only through its mean at each cost level. The definition allows arbitrary dependence between cic_ici​ and ai0a_{i0}ai0​ under the joint distribution F(θ)F(\theta)F(θ): independence gives a flat τ(c)\tau(c)τ(c), while τ′(c)>0\tau'(c)>0τ′(c)>0 is adverse selection, because cheap landowners are cheap precisely since they have little to give up by not cropping.

Two polar cases help. If everyone is additional,

τ(c)=1  for all c,\tau(c)=1\ \text{ for all } c ,τ(c)=1  for all c,

the model collapses to a textbook procurement problem with value BBB per contract. If ai0a_{i0}ai0​ were a deterministic function of cic_ici​ (a single-index model), τ(c)\tau(c)τ(c) would take only the values 0 and 1; the reduced-form estimate in equation (8), strictly between 0 and 1, rejects this. The function enters the planner's objective in equation (4), the efficiency condition in equation (5), and is generalized to multidimensional costs in equation (10).

Social surplus from contracting with landowner iii is the environmental benefit actually caused by the contract minus the real resource cost of the contract. In full, the contract changes the action from ai0a_{i0}ai0​ to ai1a_{i1}ai1​, so the benefit is B⋅(ai1−ai0)B\cdot(a_{i1}-a_{i0})B⋅(ai1​−ai0​); with perfect compliance ai1=1a_{i1}=1ai1​=1 and

SSi=B⋅(ai1−ai0)−ci=B⋅(1−ai0)−ci.SS_i=B\cdot(a_{i1}-a_{i0})-c_i=B\cdot(1-a_{i0})-c_i .SSi​=B⋅(ai1​−ai0​)−ci​=B⋅(1−ai0​)−ci​.

Here B>0B>0B>0 is the social value of land retirement (dollars per acre-year), and cic_ici​ is the landowner's cost of accepting the contract, also in dollars per acre-year: the option value of cropping she gives up over the contract period plus hassle costs. The transfer ppp does not appear because it is a pure transfer between the government and the landowner (no cost of public funds is assumed).

The equation takes two values. For an additional landowner (ai0=0a_{i0}=0ai0​=0) surplus is B−ciB-c_iB−ci​, positive when cost is below the benefit. For a non-additional landowner (ai0=1a_{i0}=1ai0​=1) surplus is −ci-c_i−ci​: nothing is gained environmentally, yet the contract still restricts her future choices, so the cost is a pure loss whenever ci>0c_i>0ci​>0. Note that cic_ici​ is a cost to a non-additional landowner too, since it includes the lost option to crop later and hassle.

Because ai0a_{i0}ai0​ is never observed for contracted landowners, SSiSS_iSSi​ cannot be conditioned on directly. Taking its expectation given cic_ici​ replaces 1−ai01-a_{i0}1−ai0​ by τ(ci)\tau(c_i)τ(ci​) from equation (1), which yields the integrand of equation (4) and the multi-contract analogue in equation (18).

This is the landowner's participation decision when offered a posted (uniform) transfer ppp for the contract. Her payoff from signing is p−cip-c_ip−ci​ and her payoff from declining is normalized to zero, because cic_ici​ is defined as the minimum transfer that makes her willing to sign, so it already nets out everything she gives up. She therefore accepts exactly when p−ci≥0p-c_i\geq 0p−ci​≥0; the weak inequality is a tie-breaking convention with no consequence when costs have a density.

The important feature is what is absent: ai0a_{i0}ai0​ does not enter. The landowner is paid ppp whether or not she would have conserved anyway, so her decision reveals her cost but not her additionality. The set of participants at price ppp is everyone with ci≤pc_i\leq pci​≤p, and its size is

q(p)=∫x∗(p;c)fC(c) dc=FC(p),q(p)=\int x^*(p;c)f_C(c)\,dc=F_C(p) ,q(p)=∫x∗(p;c)fC​(c)dc=FC​(p),

which is the supply curve of contracts; inverting it gives the marginal cost curve FC−1(q)F_C^{-1}(q)FC−1​(q) used in the graphical analysis. A posted price thus always selects from the bottom of the cost distribution, which is harmful when the lowest-cost landowners are the least additional.

The rule is the special case, for a posted price, of the monotone allocation rules that any incentive-compatible mechanism must use: the probability of contracting cannot increase in cost. It is inserted into the planner's problem in equation (4), and the wedge between it and the social criterion in equation (5) is the source of inefficiency. The multidimensional analogue of this private decision is the bidding problem in equation (12).

Start from aggregate social surplus when a uniform price ppp is posted. Each landowner contributes SSiSS_iSSi​ from equation (2) if and only if she participates, equation (3), so with a unit mass of landowners

The efficient allocation is the best allocation among those that can depend on what the planner could at most learn from the landowner, namely her cost. This is the dynamic regression discontinuity specification, estimated separately for each year relative to the auction. The outcome yigty_{igt}yigt​ is a land use share for bidder iii in auction ggg and calendar year ttt (share of her land cropped, under contract, or in natural vegetation). The running variable is the distance Sig−S‾gS_{ig}-\underline{S}_gSig​−S​g​ between the bidder's score and the auction's winning threshold; 1{Sig≥S‾g}\mathbf{1}\{S_{ig}\geq\underline{S}_g\}1{Sig​≥S​g​} indicates winning. The index r(i,t)=t−tg(i)r(i,t)=t-t_{g(i)}r(i,t)=t−tg(i)​ is event time, and fr(i,t)(⋅)f_{r(i,t)}(\cdot)fr(i,t)​(⋅) is a local-linear function of the running variable, with separate slopes on each side of the cutoff and its own shape for each event time, fit within the MSE-optimal bandwidth.

The coefficient of interest is the jump at the threshold,

βr=lim⁡S↓S‾gE[yigt∣Sig=S, r(i,t)=r]−lim⁡S↑S‾gE[yigt∣Sig=S, r(i,t)=r],\beta_{r}=\lim_{S\downarrow\underline{S}_g}\mathbb{E}\left[y_{igt}\mid S_{ig}=S,\ r(i,t)=r\right]-\lim_{S\uparrow\underline{S}_g}\mathbb{E}\left[y_{igt}\mid S_{ig}=S,\ r(i,t)=r\right],βr​=S↓S​g​lim​E[yigt​∣Sig​=S, r(i,t)=r]−S↑S​g​lim​E[yigt​∣Sig​=S, r(i,t)=r],

the effect of winning on land use rrr years after the auction for bidders at the margin. Identification rests on continuity of potential outcomes in the score at the cutoff. This is credible because the threshold is determined ex post by the acreage limit and all competing bids, so bidders cannot place themselves precisely on either side; the absence of bunching and the zero coefficients for r<0r<0r<0 (placebos) support it.

For r<0r<0r<0 the coefficients test the design, and for r>0r>0r>0 they trace the dynamics of the effect: growing over the first two years and flat afterwards. The pooled version is equation (7), and the estimates feed the additionality ratio in equation (8). The parameter is local to marginal bidders, which is why the structural model is needed to extrapolate to inframarginal ones.

This is the pooled version of equation (6): a single jump β\betaβ and a single local-linear control function f(⋅)f(\cdot)f(⋅) of the running variable, estimated on post-auction observations (r(i,t)>0r(i,t)>0r(i,t)>0) only. All symbols are as in equation (6): yigty_{igt}yigt​ is a land use share, Sig−S‾gS_{ig}-\underline{S}_gSig​−S​g​ the distance of the score from the winning threshold, and νigt\nu_{igt}νigt​ the error. Pooling imposes that the discontinuity is the same in every post-auction year, so β\betaβ is an average of the year-specific βr(i,t)\beta_{r(i,t)}βr(i,t)​ over the post-auction years observed in the five auctions of 2010-2016, weighted by their sample composition. Since the year-by-year effects are flat after the second year, little is lost and precision is gained.

Each bidder contributes several post-auction years, so the errors are correlated within bidder and the standard errors are clustered by bidder. Identification is the same as in equation (6): continuity of potential land use in the score at the cutoff.

Running the specification on different outcomes gives the ingredients of equation (8). With the outcome equal to the share of land under contract, the jump is 0.345: a first stage close to one in the probability of a contract, times the share of land offered. With the outcome equal to the share cropped, the jump is −0.075-0.075−0.075 (remote sensing) or −0.097-0.097−0.097 (administrative data). With natural vegetation and grassland it is +0.091+0.091+0.091. If every marginal winner were additional, the cropped-share jump would be

β^ cropped=−β^ contracted=−0.345,\hat{\beta}^{\,\text{cropped}}=-\hat{\beta}^{\,\text{contracted}}=-0.345 ,β^​cropped=−β^​contracted=−0.345,

and the much smaller observed value is the reduced-form evidence of limited additionality.

The ratio is a Wald (fuzzy RD) estimator: the reduced-form effect of winning on cropping divided by the first-stage effect of winning on contracted land. To see what it identifies, let ρi∈[0,1]\rho_i\in[0,1]ρi​∈[0,1] be the share of bidder iii's land she offers, so that a winner has share ρi\rho_iρi​ under contract and a loser has zero. Let 1−ai01-a_{i0}1−ai0​ be the share of the offered land she would crop without a contract. Then for a marginal bidder

contractedi(win)−contractedi(lose)=ρi.\text{contracted}_i(\text{win})-\text{contracted}_i(\text{lose})=\rho_i .contractedi​(win)−contractedi​(lose)=ρi​.

Under perfect compliance offered land is not cropped when she wins; when she loses, a share 1−ai01-a_{i0}1−ai0​ of it is cropped. If, in addition, winning does not change land use on her non-offered land (no spillovers), the difference in the cropped share of all her land is

for remote-sensing cropping, administrative cropping, and natural vegetation (with the sign reversed for the last). The derivation uses three assumptions the note states only in passing: perfect compliance, no spillovers to non-offered land (supported by the coefficient of −0.007-0.007−0.007 on nonbid fields), and a first stage of one in contract receipt. The standard error of the ratio is obtained by the delta method or by estimating the two equations jointly.

This regression is a positive-correlation test for asymmetric information. The sample is rejected bidders in the 2016 auction, for whom counterfactual land use is observed: the dependent variable 1−ai01-a_{i0}1−ai0​ is the share of bidder iii's bid fields that is cropped after losing, so it is realized additionality. The regressors are the bid characteristics bi\mathbf{b}_ibi​ (the bid rental rate and the chosen contract), other observables zi\mathbf{z}_izi​ not used in the scoring rule (for example soil productivity and prior land use), and a flexible function h(zis)h(\mathbf{z}_i^s)h(zis​) of the characteristics that the scoring rule already prices.

The logic follows the insurance literature. The bid is chosen by the landowner on the basis of her private costs, so after conditioning on everything the mechanism uses, a nonzero β\betaβ means the bid carries information about additionality that the auctioneer does not exploit:

β≠0  ⟺  E[1−ai0∣bi,zi,zis]≠E[1−ai0∣zi,zis].\beta\neq 0\iff \mathbb{E}\left[1-a_{i0}\mid\mathbf{b}_i,\mathbf{z}_i,\mathbf{z}_i^s\right]\neq\mathbb{E}\left[1-a_{i0}\mid\mathbf{z}_i,\mathbf{z}_i^s\right].β=0⟺E[1−ai0​∣bi​,zi​,zis​]=E[1−ai0​∣zi​,zis​].

A positive coefficient on the rental rate is adverse selection: landowners who demand more are more additional, which is the empirical counterpart of τ′(c)>0\tau'(c)>0τ′(c)>0 in equation (1). Coefficients on contract dummies show that contract choice reveals additionality (lower for trees), and π≠0\pi\neq 0π=0 shows that observables outside the scoring rule predict additionality and could be used for targeting.

The regression is descriptive, not causal: β\betaβ is a conditional correlation between an endogenous choice and an outcome, which is exactly what the test requires. Its limitation is selection on losing, since winners' ai0a_{i0}ai0​ is missing; with 82 percent rejected in 2016 this is mild. The coefficients motivate the structural specification in equation (17), where β\betaβ and α\alphaα load on the costs that generate the bids.

This generalizes the additionality function of equation (1) to the empirical setting, where the landowner has a vector of costs and the auctioneer observes characteristics. The conditioning set is everything a mechanism could ever screen on: the observables zi\mathbf{z}_izi​, the base cost cic_ici​ (dollars per acre-year, common to all contracts), and the vector of top-up costs κi={κij}\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i=\{\kappa_{ij}\}κi​={κij​} for the JJJ contracts. The value is the probability, or share of offered land, that would be cropped without a contract, a number in [0,1][0,1][0,1].

Two modeling choices are embedded. First, the paper does not model the cropping decision ai0a_{i0}ai0​ structurally; it models only this conditional mean. That is enough because every bid, allocation and payment in the current auction and in the counterfactuals is a function of (zi,ci,κi)(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)(zi​,ci​,κi​), so by the law of iterated expectations ai0a_{i0}ai0​ affects expected welfare only through τ\tauτ (see equation (18)). Second, the function is treated as a primitive that is invariant to the mechanism, which is valid as long as the menu of contracts is held fixed; a new contract type would change what costs mean and possibly what landowners do without a contract.

The scalar function of equation (1) is recovered by integrating out the other arguments:

τ(c)=E[τ(zi,ci,κi)∣ci=c].\tau(c)=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)\mid c_i=c\right].τ(c)=E[τ(zi​,ci​,κi​)∣ci​=c].

Dependence on cic_ici​ and κi\boldsymbol{\kappa}_iκi​ given zi\mathbf{z}_izi​ is selection on private information; dependence on zi\mathbf{z}_izi​ is heterogeneity the auctioneer can target directly. The function is parameterized linearly in equation (17) and enters welfare in equations (18) and (19).

The function G(S)G(S)G(S) is the bidder's subjective probability that a bid with score SSS wins, i.e. that SSS is at least the winning threshold S‾\underline{S}S​. Viewed as a function of SSS, it is the cumulative distribution function of the random threshold, so it is weakly increasing from 0 to 1.

The threshold is random from the bidder's perspective because it is whatever score exhausts the acreage limit once all bids are ranked. It therefore depends on the number of bidders, on their scores and offered acreages (which depend on their private costs and equilibrium strategies), and on the acreage limit itself, none of which the bidder knows when bidding. All this uncertainty is collapsed into one distribution:

G(S)=Pr⁡{S‾≤S}=FS‾(S).G(S)=\Pr\left\{\underline{S}\leq S\right\}=F_{\underline{S}}(S).G(S)=Pr{S​≤S}=FS​​(S).

Two assumptions make this a workable primitive. Beliefs are common across bidders and do not depend on the bidder's own type, which follows from costs being independent across landowners given observables. And each bidder is small (an average auction has more than 36,000 bidders), so her own bid does not move the threshold; the auction is then strategically equivalent to a single-agent problem against a fixed distribution, in the spirit of large-market approximations for multi-unit auctions.

In equation (12) GGG multiplies the payoff conditional on winning, and in equation (15) its increments determine markups. It is estimated in a first step by resampling: draw the number of bidders and the acreage limit from fitted beta distributions, resample observed scores and acreages, compute the threshold of each simulated auction, and set G(S)G(S)G(S) to the share of simulated auctions in which SSS would win. In the status quo counterfactual with a new scoring rule, GGG is recomputed as a fixed point with best responses.

This is the landowner's bidding problem. She chooses a bid consisting of a rental rate rrr (dollars per acre-year) and a contract vector x\mathbf{x}x with a single entry equal to one. If she wins she is paid her own bid rrr (the auction is discriminatory, i.e. pay-as-bid) and bears the cost ci+x⋅κic_i+\mathbf{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{\kappa}_ici​+x⋅κi​, which equals ci+κijc_i+\kappa_{ij}ci​+κij​ for the chosen contract jjj. If she loses her payoff is zero, since costs are measured relative to the outside option. The winning probability is the belief GGG from equation (11) evaluated at the score s((r,x),zis)s((r,\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{z}_i^s)s((r,x),zis​) that the scoring rule assigns to her bid given her land's scoring characteristics.

The objective is an expected profit, so bidders are risk neutral. The tradeoff is the usual first-price one, with an extra dimension: a higher rrr raises the payoff when winning but lowers the score and so the chance of winning, while a contract with more points raises the score at a top-up cost κij\kappa_{ij}κij​. With a single contract and a continuous score, the first-order condition in rrr would be the familiar markup formula

r−ci=−G(s)G′(s) ∂s/∂r,r-c_i=-\frac{G(s)}{G'(s)\,\partial s/\partial r},r−ci​=−G′(s)∂s/∂rG(s)​,

which is positive because ∂s/∂r<0\partial s/\partial r<0∂s/∂r<0: the bid exceeds cost by an information rent.

Note what is absent: ai0a_{i0}ai0​ and τ\tauτ do not enter, because the payment does not depend on counterfactual land use. Bids therefore reveal costs only. Also, acreage offered is taken as given and the payoff is per acre.

Because the win probability depends on the bid only through the score, the problem separates into the inner problem of equation (13) and the outer problem of equation (14), and the resulting inequalities, such as equation (15), invert bids into bounds on costs.

Two qualifications, both consistent with the paper. The division requires G(Si∗+1)>G(Si∗)G(S_i^*+1)>G(S_i^*)G(Si∗​+1)>G(Si∗​); if the two are equal, the upward deviation is unprofitable for any cost below the bid and yields no bound. And the formula requires the contract to be unchanged across the two scores; if the optimal contract switches, the costs on the two sides of equation (14) differ and the inequality bounds a combination of cic_ici​ and two elements of κi\boldsymbol{\kappa}_iκi​ instead.

These are the parametric assumptions on the cost distribution Fc,κ∣zF_{c,\kappa\mid z}Fc,κ∣z​. The base cost cic_ici​ is normal with mean c(zi)c(\mathbf{z}_i)c(zi​) and variance σc2(zi)\sigma_c^2(\mathbf{z}_i)σc2​(zi​), both free within each of the 32 cells of observables (soil productivity quartile by prior CRP status by prior land use). The top-up cost of contract jjj is the sum of a mean for its primary cover, pj(zi)p_j(\mathbf{z}_i)pj​(zi​), a mean for its upgrade, uj(zi)u_j(\mathbf{z}_i)uj​(zi​), and an idiosyncratic normal shock ϵij\epsilon_{ij}ϵij​, independent across contracts and of cic_ici​. All are in dollars per acre-year.

The additive structure pj+ujp_j+u_jpj​+uj​ is a dimension reduction: a contract is a pair (primary cover, upgrade), and the 36 means are generated by a handful of cover and upgrade effects. Normalizations are needed because the level of κij\kappa_{ij}κij​ is not separately identified from cic_ici​: the introduced-grass cover and "no upgrade" are set to zero, so cic_ici​ is the cost of the base contract and κij\kappa_{ij}κij​ is measured relative to it. The implied cost of contract jjj is

ci+κij∼N(c(zi)+pj(zi)+uj(zi), σc2(zi)+σκ2(zi)),c_i+\kappa_{ij}\sim N\left(c(\mathbf{z}_i)+p_j(\mathbf{z}_i)+u_j(\mathbf{z}_i),\ \sigma_c^2(\mathbf{z}_i)+\sigma_\kappa^2(\mathbf{z}_i)\right),ci​+κij​∼N(c(zi​)+pj​(zi​)+uj​(zi​), σc2​(zi​)+σκ2​(zi​)),

and costs of two contracts are positively correlated through the common cic_ici​, with covariance σc2(zi)\sigma_c^2(\mathbf{z}_i)σc2​(zi​). The base cost thus acts as a vertical type and the shocks ϵij\epsilon_{ij}ϵij​ as horizontal tastes, as in a probit with a random intercept.

Normality allows negative costs (some landowners would accept a contract for nothing) and a single common variance σκ2\sigma_\kappa^2σκ2​ rules out contract-specific dispersion. The parametric form is needed because bids reveal one score and one contract while costs have J+1J+1J+1 dimensions, and scoring-rule variation is too limited for nonparametric identification. The parameters are estimated by simulated likelihood from the inequalities in equations (13) and (14).

This is the parametric form of the additionality function defined in equation (10): a linear probability model in observables and costs. The term π⋅zi\pi\cdot\mathbf{z}_iπ⋅zi​ captures heterogeneity in additionality that the auctioneer can see; β\betaβ is the change in additionality per dollar of base cost; and α⋅κi=∑jαjκij\alpha\cdot\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i=\sum_j\alpha_j\kappa_{ij}α⋅κi​=∑j​αj​κij​ lets additionality depend on the cost of each contract type, with the αj\alpha_jαj​ restricted to be equal across contracts that share the same cover and upgrade means. Since τ\tauτ is a probability and costs are in dollars per acre-year, β\betaβ and αj\alpha_jαj​ are in probability units per dollar.

The coefficients on costs measure selection on private information. Conditional on zi\mathbf{z}_izi​,

∂τ∂ci=β,∂τ∂κij=αj,\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial c_i}=\beta,\qquad\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial\kappa_{ij}}=\alpha_j ,∂ci​∂τ​=β,∂κij​∂τ​=αj​,

so β>0\beta>0β>0 is adverse selection in the sense of equation (1): cheaper landowners are less additional. With β=0.0018\beta=0.0018β=0.0018, a landowner whose base cost is 50 dollars higher is 9 percentage points more additional, large relative to a marginal additionality of about 23 percent. A positive αj\alpha_jαj​ for trees means that those who find tree planting cheap (and hence choose it) tend to be those who would not crop anyway.

Costs are never observed, so the parameters are identified through the model: simulated costs imply bids, and the moments match observed cropping of rejected bidders by score, contract and observables, plus additionality at the threshold. Variation in bids conditional on zi\mathbf{z}_izi​ identifies β\betaβ and α\alphaα; this is the structural counterpart of the regression in equation (9).

Linearity buys transparent extrapolation from rejected bidders to winners, but it does not constrain τ\tauτ to [0,1][0,1][0,1] for extreme cost draws, and it imposes a constant slope. The function enters welfare through equations (18) and (19).

Start from realized social surplus when contract jjj is awarded to landowner iii. As in equation (2), the benefit Bj(zis)B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)Bj​(zis​) is realized only if the land would otherwise have been cropped, and the resource cost is ci+κijc_i+\kappa_{ij}ci​+κij​:

where the second line uses the definition in equation (10). This is the expression in the note.

It is "without loss" in the following sense. Let xijx_{ij}xij​ be the allocation produced by any mechanism. In the status quo auction it is a function of the bid and the threshold, and the bid is a function of (zi,ci,κi)(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)(zi​,ci​,κi​) by equation (12); in the Vickrey auctions it is a function of reported costs and observables. Expected welfare is the same whether computed with 1−ai01-a_{i0}1−ai0​ or with τ\tauτ. Two assumptions are embedded: additionality scales the entire benefit of contract jjj, including the top-up actions (the extension with B0(zis)⋅τ+Bj(zis)B_0(\mathbf{z}_i^s)\cdot\tau+B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)B0​(zis​)⋅τ+Bj​(zis​) relaxes this), and transfers have no social cost or benefit, so payments do not appear.

Welfare of an allocation is the sum, over landowners and contracts, of the expected social surplus in equation (18) for each contract actually awarded. The allocation indicator xijx_{ij}xij​ equals one if landowner iii receives contract jjj; each landowner receives at most one contract, so ∑jxij≤1\sum_j x_{ij}\leq 1∑j​xij​≤1, and the inner sum simply picks out the surplus of her awarded contract (or zero if she loses). Units are dollars per year once per-acre values are scaled by acreage; the note reports totals in million dollars per auction.

This is the single yardstick for every mechanism in the paper. The mechanisms differ only in the allocation they induce: the status quo auction awards the contracts in bids above the threshold, the Vickrey auctions with scoring award according to equation (21), and the efficient benchmark chooses xijx_{ij}xij​ to maximize WWW itself subject to one contract per landowner and no more contracts than in the status quo. Without the quantity cap the efficient rule is the multi-contract version of equation (5):

xij=1  ⟺  j=arg⁡max⁡j′{Bj′(zis)⋅τ(zi,ci,κi)−κij′} and Bj(zis)⋅τ(zi,ci,κi)−ci−κij≥0.x_{ij}=1\iff j=\arg\max_{j'}\left\{B_{j'}(\mathbf{z}_i^s)\cdot\tau(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)-\kappa_{ij'}\right\}\ \text{and}\ B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)\cdot\tau(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)-c_i-\kappa_{ij}\geq 0 .xij​=1⟺j=argj′max​{Bj′​(zis​)⋅τ(zi​,ci​,κi​)−κij′​} and Bj​(zis​)⋅τ(zi​,ci​,κi​)−ci​−κij​≥0.

Payments are absent from WWW: they are transfers, so the criterion is total surplus, not the government's budget. USDA spending is reported separately, and the welfare-weights extension asks how much a dollar to landowners would have to be worth to overturn the ranking of mechanisms.

Comparing WWW with the objective in equation (21) shows the source of inefficiency: an auction maximizes surplus as measured by its scoring rule, and this coincides with WWW only if the score equals Bj(zis)⋅τ(zi,ci,κi)B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)\cdot\tau(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)Bj​(zis​)⋅τ(zi​,ci​,κi​), which no rule based on observables can replicate when τ\tauτ depends on private costs.

This is the class of counterfactual scoring rules. The score of contract jjj for landowner iii is a linear index: weights ωz\omega_zωz​ on a vector of observable characteristics zi\mathbf{z}_izi​, plus a contract-specific intercept ωj\omega_jωj​. In the counterfactual Vickrey auctions the score is denominated in dollars per acre-year, since it is compared directly with costs in equation (21); it is the auctioneer's stated willingness to pay for contract jjj on land with characteristics zi\mathbf{z}_izi​.

The rule does not depend on the bid, on costs, or on mutable behavior. Only immutable characteristics (soil productivity, erosion indices, location) are used, so that landowners cannot game the rule by changing behavior before the auction, for instance by cropping to appear additional. The price of this restriction is that the rule cannot track the part of τ\tauτ that varies with private costs.

The benchmark the rule tries to approximate is expected contract value given observables:

sj(zi)≈E[Bj(zis)⋅τ(zi,ci,κi)∣zi, i is awarded j],s_j(\mathbf{z}_i)\approx\mathbb{E}\left[B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)\cdot\tau(\mathbf{z}_i,c_i,\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i)\mid\mathbf{z}_i,\ i\text{ is awarded }j\right],sj​(zi​)≈E[Bj​(zis​)⋅τ(zi​,ci​,κi​)∣zi​, i is awarded j],

where the conditioning on being awarded jjj matters because of selection: those who end up with contract jjj are not a random sample. The weights are chosen to maximize true welfare WWW of equation (19) given the allocation the auction induces.

The sequence of counterfactuals in the note corresponds to progressively freeing the weights: first the contract intercepts ωj\omega_jωj​ (which lowers the reward for contracts such as trees that attract non-additional landowners), then the weights ωz\omega_zωz​ on characteristics already in the rule, then adding an additionality factor τ^(zi)\hat{\tau}(\mathbf{z}_i)τ^(zi​) built from characteristics not currently used. Lowering all scores also lowers quantity once bidders with negative scored surplus are rejected. The uniform multiplier rule of equation (22) is a one-parameter alternative.

The Vickrey auction with scoring chooses the allocation xijx_{ij}xij​ that maximizes the scored surplus in the note, subject to one contract per landowner, ∑jxij≤1\sum_jx_{ij}\leq 1∑j​xij​≤1, and a quantity limit of KKK contracts, ∑i∑jxij≤K\sum_i\sum_jx_{ij}\leq K∑i​∑j​xij​≤K. This is the ranking stated in the note.

Finally compare with true welfare in equation (19):

The mechanism is efficient with respect to the score, and welfare losses arise only from the gap between the score and true expected contract value. This isolates the design of the scoring rule in equation (20) from distortions due to bid shading in the pay-as-bid format. The formula for tit_iti​ is the standard VCG payment implied by the objective; the note does not state it.

The uniform multiplier rule scales the entire status quo valuation by a single number θ\thetaθ. Here Bj(zis)B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)Bj​(zis​) is the social benefit of contract jjj on land with scoring characteristics zis\mathbf{z}_i^szis​ that is built into the existing rule under the assumption of full additionality, and θ\thetaθ is a discount applied uniformly across contracts and land types (it is unrelated to the landowner type θi\theta_iθi​ of the stylized framework). The rule is used in the Vickrey auction of equation (21), so bidders are ranked by the largest value over contracts of θ⋅Bj(zis)−ci−κij\theta\cdot B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)-c_i-\kappa_{ij}θ⋅Bj​(zis​)−ci​−κij​, and the number of contracts is held at the status quo quantity.

The rationale is seen by comparing with true welfare in equation (19). If additionality were a constant τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ for everyone, expected contract value would be τˉ⋅Bj(zis)\bar{\tau}\cdot B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)τˉ⋅Bj​(zis​) and setting

θ=τˉ⟹∑i∑j(sj(zis)−ci−κij)⋅xij=W\theta=\bar{\tau}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sum_i\sum_j\left(s_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)-c_i-\kappa_{ij}\right)\cdot x_{ij}=Wθ=τˉ⟹i∑​j∑​(sj​(zis​)−ci​−κij​)⋅xij​=W

would make the auction efficient for the given quantity. With heterogeneous additionality, the best θ\thetaθ is roughly the average additionality of the bidders near the margin of being awarded, and the rule is second best. The status quo corresponds to θ=1\theta=1θ=1.

Because quantity is held fixed, a multiplier below one does not work by buying fewer contracts. It works by changing the marginal rate of substitution between benefits and costs in the ranking: differences in Bj(zis)B_j(\mathbf{z}_i^s)Bj​(zis​) across contracts and land types shrink in proportion, so asymmetries that the status quo overweights (benefits that are not realized when land would be conserved anyway) carry less weight relative to differences in costs, and fewer landowners are steered into expensive high-point contracts.

The rule yields 325 million dollars per auction, against 349 for the heterogeneous rule of equation (20) at the same quantity: one number, the average discount for imperfect additionality, captures most of the gain, and targeting heterogeneity adds 24 million.
